extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic, and scientific methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing the logical grounds and proper scope of inductive reasoning in science, including how to distinguish genuine induction from mere description/colligation and what warrants generalization from instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction as generalization from experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction properly so called may be summarily defined as Generalization from Experience: inferring from some individual instances in which a phenomenon is observed to occur, that it occurs in all instances of a certain class, namely, in all which resemble the former in the material circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction involves drawing an inference from observed particular cases to unobserved similar cases; it is not merely restating observed facts. Example: inferring that a property found in observed animals will be found in undiscovered animals when the general proposition contains more than the sum of the special propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish description/colligation from induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The colligation (or description) of facts is the operation of combining piecemeal observations into a single general expression; this is not induction if no unobserved matter is inferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sailing round a coast to determine it's an island, or Kepler representing observed planetary positions by an ellipse — these are summaries/descriptions of observed facts, not inductions, unless one infers unobserved facts (e.g., that the planet will occupy intermediate points). Colligation is necessary preparation for induction but is distinct from it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction requires that the general proposition add more than observed particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: If the general proposition contains more than the sum of the special propositions from which it is inferred, it is an induction; if it merely rephrases 'all known' cases, it is not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimacy of a real generalization does not usually require examination of every known instance; rather, it depends on the number and nature of the instances (their sufficiency) to prove a general law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency depends on number and nature of instances, not exhaustiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: In legitimate induction it is the number and nature of the instances, and not their being the whole of those which happen to be known, that makes them sufficient evidence to prove a general law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One need not examine every known species to infer a lawful generalization if the collected instances are of the right kind and quantity to warrant the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical summation (parity of reasoning) is not induction
rubrics_metrics.description: When a truth is proved for a set of mathematical species and then summed up as a universal property (e.g., sections of a cone), the process is not induction but a summing up or 'induction by parity of reasoning'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The characteristic quality of induction — inferring unobserved facts from observed instances — is absent because the general truth is supported by demonstrative proof applicable to any particular case, not by evidence of particular instances alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extrapolation from finite pattern needs a priori justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Filling succeeding terms of a series after computing several terms is warranted only when a priori considerations show that the mode of formation will continue similarly; without such grounds it can lead to false results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: mathematicians infer later terms of a series when underlying rules (e.g., formation law) justify the extension; blind pattern-matching across few terms is risky.

rubrics_metrics.name: The generation of hypotheses is tentative and empirical (skillful guessing)
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection of a conception suitable to express facts is a tentative process: a succession of guesses, many rejected, until one fits; successful guesses are generally 'skillful' rather than merely lucky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kepler tried many hypothetical paths before selecting an ellipse; hypothesis-generation is trial-and-error informed by prior knowledge and intellectual discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceptions used for colligation must correspond to real properties in the facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A mental conception (e.g., 'ellipse') must correspond to something actually in the facts if it is to convey knowledge about them; the conception often is obtained by abstraction from the facts themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although conceptions are mental, they represent properties that would manifest in facts if observed with adequate instruments or vantage; thus conceiving a shape is discovering rather than adding to the facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction presupposes the uniformity of nature / existence of parallel cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction implicitly assumes that there are such things in nature as parallel cases: that what happens once will, under sufficient similarity of circumstances, happen again; this uniformity of nature is the warrant for inferences from experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different philosophers have expressed this as 'course of nature is uniform' or 'universe is governed by general laws'; recognizing this assumption is necessary to justify inductive moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction is concerned with explanation and prediction (not mere description)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific study of facts may be for description, explanation, or prediction; the name Induction properly belongs to explanation and prediction (determining conditions under which similar facts may be expected), not to mere description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competing descriptions may all be 'true' as representations of observed data, but competing explanations and predictions are not all true — they are judged by their explanatory/predictive correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction requires a test of proof and inductive logic (not mere guessing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is proof; it is inferring something unobserved from something observed, and therefore requires an appropriate test of proof — the special purpose of inductive logic — rather than relying solely on the guessing process of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While invention (framing conceptions) is involved in science, logical canons are needed to justify that an inductive inference really establishes a new fact (contrast with Whewell's view that invention = induction).

rubrics_metrics.name: New mental conception (invention) is not the essence of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Although introducing a new conception may be necessary for describing or hypothesizing, it is not the essence of induction; many inductions require no new conception beyond those present in particular instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'all men are mortal' is an inductive conclusion that does not introduce a novel conception; conflating invention with induction is a conceptual error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colligation is a necessary preparatory step for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction always presupposes that the results of observations are, so far as practicable, connected together by general descriptions enabling the mind to represent phenomena as wholes; without prior colligation, induction would be impossible for phenomena observed piecemeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Descriptive generalizations (colligations) provide the basis upon which inductive inferences (explanations/predictions) can be formulated and tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanations (theories) are judged differently than mere descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different descriptive generalizations (e.g., circular or epicyclic representations of orbits) may be all 'correct' as descriptions given the observational accuracy at the time, but explanations (forces, laws) are mutually exclusive in truth; only one explanatory account can be true to any degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explanatory power and truth-content (including predictive success) to prefer one explanation over another; mere convenience or simplicity of description does not establish explanatory truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish material from immaterial circumstances when generalizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction requires specifying the class of instances by their resembling the observed ones 'in what are regarded as the material circumstances'; identifying which circumstances are material is essential though not trivial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The task of determining which circumstances matter for the generalization is central to sound induction; this determination is nontrivial and must be made before reliable induction can proceed.
